How do noise-canceling headphones cancel sound?
a: Noise-canceling headphones use a technology called active noise control (ANC) to reduce unwanted ambient sounds. The process works in three steps: first, external microphones detect incoming sound waves; second, a digital signal processor analyzes these waves and generates an 'anti-noise' wave that is the exact inverse (180 degrees out of phase) of the original sound; third, this anti-noise wave is played through the headphones' speakers, where it combines with the original sound wave and cancels it out through a process called destructive interference. This is most effective for continuous low-frequency sounds like airplane engines, air conditioners, or traffic noise. For higher-frequency sounds, noise-canceling headphones also rely on passive noise isolation — the physical seal of the ear cups blocking sound from entering. The anti-noise wave must be generated in real-time, with the system continuously monitoring and adjusting to changing ambient sounds. Some advanced systems use multiple microphones and machine learning to predict and cancel noise more effectively. While active noise cancellation can reduce ambient noise by 15-30 decibels, it cannot eliminate all sound, particularly sudden, high-frequency noises like voices or door slams.

a: Active noise cancellation (ANC) works by detecting ambient sound waves with microphones, generating an inverse 'anti-noise' wave that is 180 degrees out of phase with the original sound, and playing it through the headphones to cancel the noise through destructive interference. This works best for low-frequency, continuous sounds like airplane engines.
